options.text: A single physical building that holds servers
A set of datacenters in one area, connected by a dedicated low-latency network
A boundary used to bill a team for its usage
A logical container that holds related resources

explanation: A region groups nearby datacenters on a fast private network. You pick a region when you create most resources.

why_wrong.a: That describes a datacenter, which is one building inside a region.

prompt: A company must keep its workloads in an isolated Azure instance that meets strict government compliance rules and is separate from the public Azure cloud. What should it look at?

options.text: A region pair
A sovereign region
A management group
An availability zone

explanation: Sovereign regions, such as Azure Government, are isolated instances built for legal and compliance needs.

why_wrong.a: Region pairs are about recovery across two regions in the same public cloud, not isolation.
why_wrong.d: Availability zones protect against datacenter failures inside one region.
why_wrong.c: Management groups organise subscriptions; they do not isolate the platform.

prompt: Which statement describes a benefit of Azure region pairs?

options.text: In a very large outage, Azure prioritises restoring one region in each pair
Two paired regions are billed as one region
Every Azure service is guaranteed to be available in both regions of a pair
Every resource is automatically copied to the paired region

explanation: Pairing helps recovery: if a wide outage happens, one region from each pair is restored first.

why_wrong.c: Not every service is offered in every region, paired or not.
why_wrong.b: Pairing has nothing to do with billing.
why_wrong.d: Replication to the pair is a feature of individual services, such as geo-redundant storage; it is not automatic for everything.

options.text: A segment of a virtual network
A physically separate location inside a region, with its own power, cooling and networking
Two regions in the same geography that recover together
A group of subscriptions with shared policy

explanation: Availability zones are separate locations within a region, each made of one or more datacenters with independent power, cooling and networking.

why_wrong.a: That describes a subnet, which is a networking concept.

prompt: A company runs a web app on virtual machines in one region. It wants the app to keep running if a single datacenter loses power, without moving to another region. What should it do?

options.text: Create a management group for the virtual machines
Spread the virtual machines across availability zones in the region
Move the workload to a sovereign region
Place all the virtual machines in one resource group

explanation: Zones are physically separate, so a failure in one zone leaves the others running, and you stay in the same region.

why_wrong.d: A resource group is a logical container; it gives no protection from a power failure.
why_wrong.c: Sovereign regions are for compliance isolation, not for datacenter-level resilience.
why_wrong.a: Management groups hold subscriptions, not virtual machines.

prompt: Which TWO statements about availability zones are true? (Select two.)

options.text: Availability zones are the same thing as region pairs
Each zone has its own power, cooling and networking
Zones in a region are connected by a low-latency network
The zones of a region are located in different geographies
Every Azure region supports availability zones

explanation: Zones are independent in power, cooling and networking, yet sit close enough to be joined by a fast network.

why_wrong.e: Not every region has availability zones.
why_wrong.d: Zones are inside one region, so they share a geography.
why_wrong.a: Region pairs link two regions; zones sit inside one region.

options.text: A physical rack of servers in a datacenter
A copy of a resource stored in another region
A set of users who share the same role
A logical container that holds related Azure resources

explanation: Resource groups organise resources that share a lifecycle, so you can deploy, manage and delete them together.

why_wrong.a: Racks are physical hardware inside datacenters.
why_wrong.b: Copying a resource to another region is replication, not grouping.
why_wrong.c: Groups of users are handled by identity and access features.

prompt: Decide whether each statement about resource groups is true.

options.text: A resource can belong to more than one resource group at the same time.
Deleting a resource group deletes the resources inside it.
A resource group can contain resources that are in different regions.

explanation: Each resource lives in exactly one group, deleting a group removes its contents, and the group's location only stores metadata, so its resources can be in other regions.

why_wrong.s1: No. A resource belongs to exactly one resource group.
why_wrong.s2: Yes. Deleting the group deletes everything in it, so be careful.
why_wrong.s3: Yes. The group's location only says where its metadata is kept.

prompt: A large organisation has many subscriptions and wants to apply the same policy and access rules to all of them at once. What should it use?

options.text: Management groups
Availability zones
Region pairs
Resource groups

explanation: Management groups sit above subscriptions, and what you apply to them is inherited by every subscription beneath.

why_wrong.d: Resource groups sit below subscriptions and hold resources.
why_wrong.b: Availability zones are about physical resilience, not governance.
why_wrong.c: Region pairs are about recovery across regions.

prompt: Decide whether each statement about the Azure hierarchy is true.

options.text: A subscription can contain management groups.
Policy applied to a management group is inherited by the subscriptions beneath it.
A subscription is a boundary for both billing and access control.

explanation: Management groups contain subscriptions, not the reverse. Inheritance flows downward, and a subscription is both a billing and an access boundary.

why_wrong.s1: No. Management groups contain subscriptions; a subscription cannot contain a management group.
why_wrong.s2: Yes. Settings applied at a management group flow down to its subscriptions.
why_wrong.s3: Yes. Subscriptions are where usage is billed and where access is controlled.

prompt: Which TWO levels sit between a management group and an individual resource in the Azure hierarchy? (Select two.)

options.text: Resource provider
Resource group
Subscription
Availability zone
Region

explanation: The order is management group, then subscription, then resource group, then resource.

why_wrong.e: A region is a physical location, not a level of the management hierarchy.
why_wrong.d: An availability zone is a physical location inside a region, not a hierarchy level.
why_wrong.a: A resource provider supplies a type of resource; it is not a hierarchy level.

prompt: Which list shows Azure physical infrastructure from smallest to largest?

options.text: Region, availability zone, datacenter
Availability zone, datacenter, region
Datacenter, region, availability zone
Datacenter, availability zone, region

explanation: Datacenters make up availability zones (a zone has one or more), and zones sit inside a region.

why_wrong.b: A zone is made of datacenters, so a datacenter is smaller than a zone.
why_wrong.c: Zones are inside a region, so a zone comes before a region.

prompt: A company wants separate billing and separate access control for its development and production environments. What should it create?

options.text: Separate availability zones
Separate region pairs
Separate datacenters
Separate subscriptions

explanation: A subscription is both a billing boundary and an access-control boundary, so separate subscriptions separate both.

why_wrong.a: Availability zones are about physical resilience, not billing or access.
why_wrong.b: Region pairs are about recovery across regions, not billing.
why_wrong.c: Datacenters are physical buildings run by Microsoft; you do not create them.

prompt: What do you need before you can create resources in Azure?

options.text: A dedicated datacenter
An Azure subscription, which is created with your Azure account
A management group
An availability zone

explanation: Resources are created inside a subscription.

why_wrong.c: Management groups are optional organisation tools.
why_wrong.d: Availability zones are optional resilience features.

prompt: What does the Azure free account offer new users?

options.text: Unlimited use of every Azure service with no end date
A discount that applies only to reserved virtual machines
A one-hour trial of the portal only
Free access to popular products for 12 months, a first-30-days credit and some always-free services

explanation: The free account combines a 12-month offer, an initial credit and always-free services.

why_wrong.a: The free account has limits and an end to the credit.
why_wrong.c: It is far broader than a one-hour trial.
why_wrong.b: It is not tied to reservations.

prompt: Decide whether each statement is true.

options.text: Creating an Azure account creates a subscription for you.
You can create additional subscriptions, such as development, testing and production.
A free account charges your payment card as soon as you sign up.

explanation: An account comes with a subscription and can have more; the card on a free account is for identity verification until you upgrade.

why_wrong.s1: Yes. A subscription is created for you.
why_wrong.s2: Yes. Many organisations use separate subscriptions per environment.
why_wrong.s3: No. You are not charged until you upgrade to a paid subscription.
